report.headline: Usage projected to shrink well below NBA average, and shooting projection carries no signal

projection.text: Player A's usage rate is projected to fall to 14.1% in the NBA, down from 17.6% in the G League and below the NBA's minutes-weighted average of 20.1%.

risks.text: The projected 14.1% usage rate sits roughly 1.2 standard deviations below the NBA average of 20.1% (SD 5.2%), pointing to a materially reduced offensive role.
He was 27 years old in the source season and his usage rate there was already 0.50 standard deviations below the G League average, an older, lower-usage profile heading into the move.
The true shooting projection of 52.5%, below both his source-season mark and the NBA average, cannot be trusted since the model underperforms a naive league-average baseline on this metric.
The 95% prediction interval for usage rate spans 6.1% to 22.1%, covering nearly the full range of plausible NBA roles from bit-part to above-average.

strengths.text: In the source G League season he produced 15.7 points, 5.1 rebounds, and 2.3 assists per 75 possessions across 50 games and 1,463 minutes.
He shot efficiently, posting a 56.4% true shooting percentage, about 0.19 standard deviations above the G League average, on a heavy diet of threes (53.1% of attempts) with a low 9.4% turnover rate.
He belongs to a cohort of G League to NBA movers who sat 0.27 standard deviations above their own league's average, the group this model's projections are conditioned on.
Usage rate historically retains about 53.1% of a player's standing across this specific transition, giving the projection some grounding despite the wide interval.

uncertainty.text: The 80% prediction interval for usage rate runs from 8.8% to 19.3%, a span of roughly two standard deviations of the NBA usage distribution (SD 5.2%), so the model can rank this player against peers but cannot pin down an individual value; the 95% interval widens further to 6.1%-22.1%. The true shooting projection of 52.5% should not be read as informative at all, since the model's held-out error (4.7%) is no better than simply guessing the league average (also 4.7%).
